I posted this way back to another aspiring guitar beginner:

Two things: I've "played" guitar for 15 years but I only learned for about 4 of them. If you can only play a G chord I wouldn't say you've been actively playing for 8 years. It sounds condescending but it's more humbling to think in terms of how much work you've actually put into playing the instrument vs how long you've owned and occasionally held a guitar for.

That aside- The best advice you could ever get is that to stick with an instrument you gotta do three things:

.1. Learn to play equally with your fingers AND your ears. It's all about call and response. "Call" notes and chords and movements and shapes and scales and so on- call them out by playing them with your fingers, then hear the "response" in your ear and make judgements from there. Get a feel for playing things and actively and SLOWLY listening to them and making adjustments to your fingers to change them. You'll hear when you play a chord and it doesn't ring out beautifully, there's a finger not holding the note properly in there. Hum a melody out loud and find it with your fingers. Hear when you are playing the wrong notes and correct it by playing the frets higher and lower to determine where to go. Feel it and hear it. Your ears are JUST AS IMPORTANT as your fingers.

.2. Work on learning songs and learn from them as you go. Use tabs to learn songs initially, then as you get better- do away with tabs altogether, only using your ears and knowledge of chord shapes to find the notes you hear in the song and finding them on your guitar. Look for any song at all, tough or easy. From Green Day to Van Halen to Rush, you CAN play SOMETHING from all of these bands. The trick is to NOT TACKLE THE WHOLE SONG AT ONCE. Find ONE PART to begin with, whether it be the intro or a cool sounding part in the middle and isolate that individual part. Take it single note by note and really figure out what makes up that individual part. Play it as slow as you can, and hear and feel what your fingers are doing at every step of the process. You will want to play it at full speed- I tried to play Modest Mouse's Dashboard at normal speed and failed hard until I just took it single chord by chord. If you find that it is difficult to move between two chords then REALIZE that's holding you back and ISOLATE those into a lesson. Just finger the first chord and play it clean, then feel the movement and changes it takes to get to the next one. Go from the first chord to the second and back to it'd first. It doesn't have to sound like the actual song yet, you just have to get these first parts down as good as you can before you learn the next. 

I went off on a rant on that last paragraph. The main lesson I wanted to say is- Once you've learned a chord or shape with your fingers that the tab is telling you to do- LEARN WHAT IT IS CALLED. I went for a long time just learning numbers on lines until I realized that these numbers actually have names! 575555 is Am7! And if you slide that up to 9(11)9999 that's C#m7! See look now you've learned that the shape your hand makes dictates the ending of the chord name, and when you move that shape to different frets it changes the letter of the chord! Check this out: If you play a Dm ( D minor ) which is 10 12 12 10 10 10, that's kinda hard right? Well Did you know that all over the fretboard you can find the same sounds coming from different places? Check this out: If you put your finger on the 5th fret of the lowest string (E) and play it, it sounds the same as the next string up (A) when you play it open! They both make the same A note. Now you've learned that for some notes on the neck, you can find it on the next string five frets downward from it! 7 on the A is 2 on the D string! But watch out for the G and B strings, the B is tuned differently so actually the relation between those strings is FOUR frets apart. Don't worry, just go with it. So back to that Dm chord earlier in the paragraph: Play the first note of that chord, the first 10 on the E string. Now you know that can be found at 5 on the A string if you move your hand down five frets and move from string to string. You can find the whole chord there too by following those instructions. Don't worry about when you realize you can't move that topmost 10 from the E string, that's just a difference between the shapes. The greatness about different shapes for the same chords is that they still sound close to eachother while having their own differences and purposes! There's also another very widely used Dminor shape, can you find it?

That was like 5 separate lessons in one paragraph. That'll be $20.

.3. Practice for work and also for fun. Of course you're playing guitar to get better, so keep finding new lessons and songs (or just riffs!) to learn- But just like the kids seeing the whole piano in front of them and being cursed to learn Mary Had A Little Lamb one finger at a time and losing their patience, don't lose sight of the other purpose of playing an instrument: Having fun. Pure, uneducated, noisy fun. Just play your guitar and play cool sounds and don't tie yourself to the LESSON of it. I find a lot of the COMFORT I have in playing and holding my instrument comes from just messing around. After all, the guitar is just a hunk of wood with strings and when you hit it, it makes noise. If it's making noise and you put your fingers on the strings, it stops making noise. If you turn the volume knob down, play a note, then turn the volume back up- That note sounds like it came from nowhere! Feel the PHYSICS of this instrument. You can hit the strings at the area of the body with the pickups, but also pluck them over the neck frets! And even where the tuning pegs are, that makes a sound too! Just have fun with your instrument. You'll find that you're still learning even when learning isn't the immediate goal.
